Plain-language glossary — what the terms mean

Definitions explain terms, not which data products are available for your field. Scientific descriptions are paraphrased from linked sources; model-specific definitions describe SoilSense assumptions.

Water allowance (Irrigation allocation)

The amount of irrigation water allowed for a stated period and area. It is a limit, not proof that water was pumped.

SoilSense’s limited-water mode assumes about 10 inches per crop season; confirm legal annual limits and well capacity locally.

Kansas DWR Water Law Basics (opens a new tab)
Rain compared with usual (Rainfall anomaly)

How rainfall differs from a stated historical baseline for the same calendar window.

Always check the baseline years, window and units. A low total alone does not establish crop loss.

SoilSense model assumptions (opens a new tab)
Try a past weather year (Historical replay / hindcast)

Run the model with weather recorded in a past year while keeping the stated soil, costs and water assumptions fixed.

A modeled result is not an observed field harvest, a next-season forecast or a promise of a rank reversal.

SoilSense model assumptions (opens a new tab)
Weather for a broad area (Regional grid estimate)

A satellite or model product represents an area around a location rather than a weather station in that field.

A point selection does not make the native grid field-resolution. Check the product’s spatial support.

NASA POWER methodology (opens a new tab)
Water returned to the air (Evapotranspiration (ET))

Water evaporating from soil and other surfaces plus water released by plants.

ET includes water supplied by rain and soil storage; it is not irrigation pumping. Reference ET, modeled crop demand and measured/estimated actual ET are different quantities.

USGS Evapotranspiration and the Water Cycle (opens a new tab)
Water around plant roots (Root-zone soil moisture)

An estimate of water in the part of the soil where roots obtain water.

POWER root-zone wetness is a land-model estimate, not a probe reading from this field. A percentile is a comparison with history, not percent of water rights remaining.

NASA POWER methodology (opens a new tab)
Green plant signal (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI))

A unitless comparison of near-infrared and red reflected light used to describe green vegetation.

Low or missing NDVI does not prove bare soil, missing residue, drought damage or a particular crop. Clouds, season and pixel mixing matter.

NASA HLS Vegetation Indices (opens a new tab)
Possible crop-residue signal (Normalized Difference Tillage Index (NDTI))

A shortwave-infrared index used in research to estimate residue cover under suitable calibration and masking.

Not a direct residue measurement. NDTI is not an implemented SoilSense data layer merely because it is defined here. Green plants, moisture, clouds and soil can affect it.

Estimates of Conservation Tillage Practices Using Landsat Archive (opens a new tab)
Accumulated growing warmth (Growing degree days (GDD))

Heat accumulated above a crop-specific base temperature to help describe development. SoilSense’s headline indicator uses base 50°F and cap 86°F.

A modeled crop stage is not observed planting, flowering or harvest. Different crops and varieties need different heat totals.

K-State growing-degree-day research (opens a new tab)
How easily soil can erode (Soil erodibility)

A soil property describing susceptibility to detachment and transport under specified conditions.

Water-erosion K factors and wind-erodibility measures are not interchangeable. Neither alone is an erosion rate or measured soil loss.

USDA NRCS Erosion (opens a new tab)
Money after listed costs (Margin / estimated net return)

Modeled crop revenue minus the costs included in the model, usually in dollars per acre per year.

Not guaranteed profit or a complete farm accounts statement. Check which costs, yield assumptions and prices are included.

SoilSense model assumptions (opens a new tab)
Regional drought class (U.S. Drought Monitor category)

A weekly expert-blended map: D0 is abnormally dry; D1 moderate, D2 severe, D3 extreme and D4 exceptional drought.

D0 is not a drought category. A regional class is context, not proof of stress or loss on an individual field.

What is the U.S. Drought Monitor? (opens a new tab)
Water reported as used (Reported annual water use)

A historical report of water used during a stated year; Kansas requires reporting by water-right or permit holders.

A reported volume is not the legal water right, an allocation, current well capacity or current pumping.

Kansas DWR Water Law Basics (opens a new tab)
Estimated point in crop growth (Modeled crop stage / phenology)

A reference calendar or heat-based model suggests where a crop may be in its development.

It is not an observation of this field. Confirm sowing dates, variety, emergence and stage locally.

SoilSense model assumptions (opens a new tab)
Time between freezes (Frost-free season)

Days between the last spring freeze and the first fall freeze, using daily minimum air temperature at or below 32°F.

A regional temperature estimate is not a field frost observation or a forecast. Crop sensitivity and local low spots matter.

SoilSense model assumptions (opens a new tab)
Rain minus water demand (Climatic water balance)

The displayed weather indicator subtracts modeled crop water demand from rain for the stated window.

It is not a full field water budget, measured pumping or a water right. Soil storage, runoff and actual irrigation need separate treatment.

Why we suggest this
Growing-season warmth (May–Sep) is rising: +68.4 heat units per decade since 1991.
Replaying 35 years of NASA weather (shifted to today's trends) with soil water carried from the crop before, soybean in this rotation would have been stressed in about 0 of 35 years (irrigated).

How this plan builds your soil

Plain-language soil science behind this plan:

🌱
Adds nitrogen. Soybean is a legume: bacteria on its roots pull nitrogen from the air, so it needs no nitrogen fertilizer and leaves some for the next crop.
🌱
Adds nitrogen. A hairy vetch cover crop is a legume that adds a lot of nitrogen, enough to cut fertilizer for the following corn.
🍂
Leaves residue. Corn leaves a lot of stalks and leaves on the field, which protect the surface and feed soil organic matter, but it needs the most nitrogen fertilizer.
🔄
Review rotation effects. This plan has 2 different crops in 3 years. Pest effects depend on the pest, crop sequence, region and field history; diversity alone is not a promise of protection.

Local applicability — assumptions to review

Reference calendars are assumptions, not observed field phenology. Regional grids, soil survey map units and county harvests cannot establish field-specific performance. Kansas pest evidence may not transfer to other regions.

Heat stress uses extreme-heat degree days above each crop's threshold (the measure used in Schlenker & Roberts, PNAS 2009); irrigation is assumed to remove about two-thirds of heat damage.
Climate history is shifted to today's conditions only where a trend is statistically significant (Mann-Kendall, p < 0.05).
Years from the last decade count twice when scoring climate fit.
A crop-year counts as stressed when its combined water, heat, season-length and planting-condition score falls below 0.6.
Each 3-year plan is replayed against every run of consecutive NASA weather years, carrying soil water from one season to the next: crops draw stored water down, and between crops the soil stores about 50% of cool-season (Nov–Mar) rain and 15% of warm-season rain. A winter cover crop uses about 40% of that recharge.
Effective in-season rainfall = 75% of season rain; the soil can hold 80% of its available water capacity, to 2 m or the depth of the soil.
Yield = water-unlimited potential × the share of the crop's water need that was met (a water-production function, with no grain below a crop-specific minimum) × heat, season-length and planting stress.
Yield potential: dry Plains states use approximate irrigated-practice yields; other states use state (or USDA NASS county) averages × 1.1, since average farm yields reach about 85–90% of potential.
Nitrogen, seed and other input costs scale with the expected yield (yield-goal method), so low-yield rain-fed crops are budgeted more cheaply.
Fallow (a season with no crop, only weed control at about $45/acre) is offered only on rain-fed fields with under about 25 inches of rain a year.
Irrigated fields: water need is met and about $110/acre pumping cost is added.
Prices, costs, yield potentials and rotation yield effects are approximate defaults in src/engine/crops.ts and src/engine/regions.ts; replace them with local budgets.
Winter wheat cannot be sown for the first plan year once its fall planting window has passed.
Water: full irrigation. Pumping costs about $8 per inch of water per acre.
Bad years out of 10: how often a crop would have been badly stressed when replayed through the 35 years of NASA weather (shifted to today's climate trends), averaged over the plan's crops.
Yield potential is calibrated to real USDA NASS harvests for irrigated fields: recent average ÷ the share of potential the model says recent weather allowed (kept within 60–115% of the state value).
Corn yield basis: USDA Southwest district average for irrigated fields, 3 reports up to 2018.
Soybean yield basis: county average for 2 recent years × 103% (how irrigated fields compared with all fields in 10 years of county records).
Winter wheat yield basis: USDA Southwest district average for irrigated fields, 4 reports up to 2019.
Grain sorghum yield basis: county average for 2 recent years × 154% (how irrigated fields compared with all fields in 17 years of county records).
Prices: USDA NASS prices received, average of the latest months — corn $4.19/bu (state, 12 months to Sep 2026), soybean $10.88/bu (state, 12 months to Sep 2026), winter wheat $5.38/bu (state, 12 months to Sep 2026), oats $3.14/bu (national, 12 months to Sep 2026), alfalfa (hay) $123.83/ton (state, 12 months to Sep 2026), grain sorghum $3.62/bu (state, 12 months to Sep 2026). What the satellite measures mean
Green plant signal ⓘ
A unitless comparison of near-infrared and red reflected light used to describe green vegetation. Low or missing NDVI does not prove bare soil, missing residue, drought damage or a particular crop. Clouds, season and pixel mixing matter.
NASA MODIS greenness map layer; availability and quality must be checked separately
Water returned to the air ⓘ
Water evaporating from soil and other surfaces plus water released by plants. ET includes water supplied by rain and soil storage; it is not irrigation pumping. Reference ET, modeled crop demand and measured/estimated actual ET are different quantities.
Modeled demand from daily temperature; OpenET actual-ET estimates where available
Water around plant roots ⓘ
An estimate of water in the part of the soil where roots obtain water. POWER root-zone wetness is a land-model estimate, not a probe reading from this field. A percentile is a comparison with history, not percent of water rights remaining.
NASA POWER root-zone wetness; NASA SMAP map layer
Rain minus water demand ⓘ
The displayed weather indicator subtracts modeled crop water demand from rain for the stated window. It is not a full field water budget, measured pumping or a water right. Soil storage, runoff and actual irrigation need separate treatment.
Rain minus modeled demand, May–September
Time between freezes ⓘ
Days between the last spring freeze and the first fall freeze, using daily minimum air temperature at or below 32°F. A regional temperature estimate is not a field frost observation or a forecast. Crop sensitivity and local low spots matter.
NASA daily minimum temperatures
Accumulated growing warmth ⓘ
Heat accumulated above a crop-specific base temperature to help describe development. SoilSense’s headline indicator uses base 50°F and cap 86°F. A modeled crop stage is not observed planting, flowering or harvest. Different crops and varieties need different heat totals.
Accumulated warmth from daily NASA temperature
Rain compared with usual ⓘ
How rainfall differs from a stated historical baseline for the same calendar window. Always check the baseline years, window and units. A low total alone does not establish crop loss.

Satellite data vs. measurements on the ground

Satellite and model data (NASA POWER, MODIS, SMAP) cover every field on Earth, every day, for decades, and cost nothing. But one value stands for a large square: about 30 miles for our weather, 6 miles for SMAP soil moisture, 800 feet for MODIS plant greenness.

Ground measurements (a rain gauge, a soil probe, a soil test) are exact for one spot, but most fields have none, and few go back 35 years.

What that means for you: use this plan for the big picture, such as which crops fit your climate and how it is shifting. If you have a rain gauge or a soil test, trust it over our numbers for your field. We use the USDA soil survey because it was mapped on the ground.

USDA NRCS SSURGO (Soil Data Access) — Soil type, drainage, pH, organic matter, water-holding capacity
NASA Daymet (ORNL DAAC, 1 km daily) — Rain and temperature at the field, averaged with NASA POWER
USDA NASS Quick Stats — Real county and district harvests by practice (irrigated / rain-fed), and current state crop prices
USDA RMA Cause of Loss — Crop-insurance payouts by cause (drought, flood, hail, wind…) for the county since 1991
OpenET (NASA/USGS Landsat) — Measured crop water use on the field since 2016, to check our water model
FCC Area API — County lookup
Heat stress uses extreme-heat degree days above each crop's threshold (the measure used in Schlenker & Roberts, PNAS 2009); irrigation is assumed to remove about two-thirds of heat damage.
Climate history is shifted to today's conditions only where a trend is statistically significant (Mann-Kendall, p < 0.05).
Years from the last decade count twice when scoring climate fit.
A crop-year counts as stressed when its combined water, heat, season-length and planting-condition score falls below 0.6.
Each 3-year plan is replayed against every run of consecutive NASA weather years, carrying soil water from one season to the next: crops draw stored water down, and between crops the soil stores about 50% of cool-season (Nov–Mar) rain and 15% of warm-season rain. A winter cover crop uses about 40% of that recharge.
Effective in-season rainfall = 75% of season rain; the soil can hold 80% of its available water capacity, to 2 m or the depth of the soil.
Yield = water-unlimited potential × the share of the crop's water need that was met (a water-production function, with no grain below a crop-specific minimum) × heat, season-length and planting stress.
Yield potential: dry Plains states use approximate irrigated-practice yields; other states use state (or USDA NASS county) averages × 1.1, since average farm yields reach about 85–90% of potential.
Nitrogen, seed and other input costs scale with the expected yield (yield-goal method), so low-yield rain-fed crops are budgeted more cheaply.
Fallow (a season with no crop, only weed control at about $45/acre) is offered only on rain-fed fields with under about 25 inches of rain a year.
Irrigated fields: water need is met and about $110/acre pumping cost is added.
Prices, costs, yield potentials and rotation yield effects are approximate defaults in src/engine/crops.ts and src/engine/regions.ts; replace them with local budgets.
Winter wheat cannot be sown for the first plan year once its fall planting window has passed.
Water: full irrigation. Pumping costs about $8 per inch of water per acre.
Bad years out of 10: how often a crop would have been badly stressed when replayed through the 35 years of NASA weather (shifted to today's climate trends), averaged over the plan's crops.
Yield potential is calibrated to real USDA NASS harvests for irrigated fields: recent average ÷ the share of potential the model says recent weather allowed (kept within 60–115% of the state value).
Corn yield basis: USDA Southwest district average for irrigated fields, 3 reports up to 2018.
Soybean yield basis: county average for 2 recent years × 103% (how irrigated fields compared with all fields in 10 years of county records).
Winter wheat yield basis: USDA Southwest district average for irrigated fields, 4 reports up to 2019.
Grain sorghum yield basis: county average for 2 recent years × 154% (how irrigated fields compared with all fields in 17 years of county records).
Prices: USDA NASS prices received, average of the latest months — corn $4.19/bu (state, 12 months to Sep 2026), soybean $10.88/bu (state, 12 months to Sep 2026), winter wheat $5.38/bu (state, 12 months to Sep 2026), oats $3.14/bu (national, 12 months to Sep 2026), alfalfa (hay) $123.83/ton (state, 12 months to Sep 2026), grain sorghum $3.62/bu (state, 12 months to Sep 2026). Other prices are defaults.
This area averages about 21 inches of rain a year; fallow was not considered.
Replayed past years are history, not a forecast: each uses that year's real NASA weather on this soil, compared with what the county really harvested (USDA NASS) and why crop insurance paid out (USDA RMA).

How we check ourselves

Recorded out-of-sample test: model frozen before evaluation, 13 previously unseen counties, 43 county–crop cases, four crops, 12–35 years per case. These compare detrended county yields with historical model estimates, not next-season forecasts.

0.41 average Pearson correlation
42 of 43 cases: positive correlation (right direction)
33 of 43 cases beat rainfall-only (0.41 vs 0.21 average)

DATA SOURCES

Where our data comes from

Every plan is built from free, public data from NASA and the US government. Here is each source, what we take from it, and what it does in your plan.

Field data

We look these up live for the exact spot you pick, then cache the results so repeat visits are fast.

NASA POWER

NASA Langley Research Center

Daily weather for any point on Earth, built from NASA satellite and weather-model data (MERRA-2). It covers 1991 to last year.

DATA WE GET
Daily rainfall
Daily average, high and low temperature
Root-zone soil wetness
WHAT IT DOES

This is the core of every plan. From it we work out frost-free days, growing degree days, hot days of 95 °F or more, spring rain, summer dry spells and summer highs. Then we test which of those are really changing on your field.

Visit source ↗
Daymet

NASA Oak Ridge National Laboratory DAAC

Daily weather for North America on a fine 1-kilometer grid, built from weather stations. It covers 1991 to last year.

DATA WE GET
Daily rainfall
Daily high and low temperature
WHAT IT DOES

We average it with NASA POWER for every weather calculation. Two independent NASA datasets agree better with real harvests than either one alone.

Visit source ↗
SSURGO soil survey

USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service

The official US soil map. It is drawn field by field from on-the-ground soil surveys.

DATA WE GET
Soil name and type
Drainage class
pH
Organic matter
Clay and sand content
Water-holding capacity
WHAT IT DOES

This shows how much water your soil can store for dry spells, and which crops suit your soil.

Visit source ↗
Cropland Data Layer (CropScape)

USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service

A satellite map of what was planted on every 30-meter square of US farmland, made every year.

DATA WE GET
What crop grew on your field in each of the last 6 years
WHAT IT DOES

It shows your recent rotation, so the plan follows on from what you actually grew and avoids repeating crops.

Visit source ↗

Federal Communications Commission

Turns a map point into a US county.

County name
State
County code (FIPS)
WHAT IT DOES

We use it to label your field and match it to county-level farm statistics.

Official USDA farm survey results.

County yields, split into irrigated and rain-fed
Crop prices farmers received over the last 12 months

Sets realistic yields for how your field is farmed, uses current prices for the profit estimates, and provides the real harvests we check our model against.

Crop insurance payouts in each county, by crop, year and cause.

What hurt each crop in each year: drought, flood, hail, wind, freeze or pests

Labels the worst harvest years with their real cause, explains years our weather model misses (like the 2020 Iowa windstorm), and adds a "what hurts this crop here" reason.

Plain-language glossary — what the terms mean

Definitions explain terms, not which data products are available for your field. Scientific descriptions are paraphrased from linked sources; model-specific definitions describe SoilSense assumptions.

Water allowance (Irrigation allocation)

The amount of irrigation water allowed for a stated period and area. It is a limit, not proof that water was pumped.

SoilSense’s limited-water mode assumes about 10 inches per crop season; confirm legal annual limits and well capacity locally.

Kansas DWR Water Law Basics (opens a new tab)
Rain compared with usual (Rainfall anomaly)

How rainfall differs from a stated historical baseline for the same calendar window.

Always check the baseline years, window and units. A low total alone does not establish crop loss.

SoilSense model assumptions (opens a new tab)
Try a past weather year (Historical replay / hindcast)

Run the model with weather recorded in a past year while keeping the stated soil, costs and water assumptions fixed.

A modeled result is not an observed field harvest, a next-season forecast or a promise of a rank reversal.

SoilSense model assumptions (opens a new tab)
Weather for a broad area (Regional grid estimate)

A satellite or model product represents an area around a location rather than a weather station in that field.

A point selection does not make the native grid field-resolution. Check the product’s spatial support.

NASA POWER methodology (opens a new tab)
Water returned to the air (Evapotranspiration (ET))

Water evaporating from soil and other surfaces plus water released by plants.

ET includes water supplied by rain and soil storage; it is not irrigation pumping. Reference ET, modeled crop demand and measured/estimated actual ET are different quantities.

USGS Evapotranspiration and the Water Cycle (opens a new tab)
Water around plant roots (Root-zone soil moisture)

An estimate of water in the part of the soil where roots obtain water.

POWER root-zone wetness is a land-model estimate, not a probe reading from this field. A percentile is a comparison with history, not percent of water rights remaining.

NASA POWER methodology (opens a new tab)
Green plant signal (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI))

A unitless comparison of near-infrared and red reflected light used to describe green vegetation.

Low or missing NDVI does not prove bare soil, missing residue, drought damage or a particular crop. Clouds, season and pixel mixing matter.

NASA HLS Vegetation Indices (opens a new tab)
Possible crop-residue signal (Normalized Difference Tillage Index (NDTI))

A shortwave-infrared index used in research to estimate residue cover under suitable calibration and masking.

Not a direct residue measurement. NDTI is not an implemented SoilSense data layer merely because it is defined here. Green plants, moisture, clouds and soil can affect it.

Estimates of Conservation Tillage Practices Using Landsat Archive (opens a new tab)
Accumulated growing warmth (Growing degree days (GDD))

Heat accumulated above a crop-specific base temperature to help describe development. SoilSense’s headline indicator uses base 50°F and cap 86°F.

A modeled crop stage is not observed planting, flowering or harvest. Different crops and varieties need different heat totals.

K-State growing-degree-day research (opens a new tab)
How easily soil can erode (Soil erodibility)

A soil property describing susceptibility to detachment and transport under specified conditions.

Water-erosion K factors and wind-erodibility measures are not interchangeable. Neither alone is an erosion rate or measured soil loss.

USDA NRCS Erosion (opens a new tab)
Money after listed costs (Margin / estimated net return)

Modeled crop revenue minus the costs included in the model, usually in dollars per acre per year.

Not guaranteed profit or a complete farm accounts statement. Check which costs, yield assumptions and prices are included.

SoilSense model assumptions (opens a new tab)
Regional drought class (U.S. Drought Monitor category)

A weekly expert-blended map: D0 is abnormally dry; D1 moderate, D2 severe, D3 extreme and D4 exceptional drought.

D0 is not a drought category. A regional class is context, not proof of stress or loss on an individual field.

What is the U.S. Drought Monitor? (opens a new tab)
Water reported as used (Reported annual water use)

A historical report of water used during a stated year; Kansas requires reporting by water-right or permit holders.

A reported volume is not the legal water right, an allocation, current well capacity or current pumping.

Kansas DWR Water Law Basics (opens a new tab)
Estimated point in crop growth (Modeled crop stage / phenology)

A reference calendar or heat-based model suggests where a crop may be in its development.

It is not an observation of this field. Confirm sowing dates, variety, emergence and stage locally.

SoilSense model assumptions (opens a new tab)
Time between freezes (Frost-free season)

Days between the last spring freeze and the first fall freeze, using daily minimum air temperature at or below 32°F.

A regional temperature estimate is not a field frost observation or a forecast. Crop sensitivity and local low spots matter.

SoilSense model assumptions (opens a new tab)
Rain minus water demand (Climatic water balance)

The displayed weather indicator subtracts modeled crop water demand from rain for the stated window.

It is not a full field water budget, measured pumping or a water right. Soil storage, runoff and actual irrigation need separate treatment.

SoilSense model assumptions (opens a new tab)

How this plan builds your soil

Plain-language soil science behind this plan:

🌱
Adds nitrogen. Soybean is a legume: bacteria on its roots pull nitrogen from the air, so it needs no nitrogen fertilizer and leaves some for the next crop.
🌱
Adds nitrogen. A hairy vetch cover crop is a legume that adds a lot of nitrogen, enough to cut fertilizer for the following corn.
🍂
Leaves residue. Corn leaves a lot of stalks and leaves on the field, which protect the surface and feed soil organic matter, but it needs the most nitrogen fertilizer.
🔄
Review rotation effects. This plan has 2 different crops in 3 years. Pest effects depend on the pest, crop sequence, region and field history; diversity alone is not a promise of protection.

Local applicability — assumptions to review

Reference calendars are assumptions, not observed field phenology. Regional grids, soil survey map units and county harvests cannot establish field-specific performance. Kansas pest evidence may not transfer to other regions.

Heat stress uses extreme-heat degree days above each crop's threshold (the measure used in Schlenker & Roberts, PNAS 2009); irrigation is assumed to remove about two-thirds of heat damage.
Climate history is shifted to today's conditions only where a trend is statistically significant (Mann-Kendall, p < 0.05).
Years from the last decade count twice when scoring climate fit.
A crop-year counts as stressed when its combined water, heat, season-length and planting-condition score falls below 0.6.
Each 3-year plan is replayed against every run of consecutive NASA weather years, carrying soil water from one season to the next: crops draw stored water down, and between crops the soil stores about 50% of cool-season (Nov–Mar) rain and 15% of warm-season rain. A winter cover crop uses about 40% of that recharge.
Effective in-season rainfall = 75% of season rain; the soil can hold 80% of its available water capacity, to 2 m or the depth of the soil.
Yield = water-unlimited potential × the share of the crop's water need that was met (a water-production function, with no grain below a crop-specific minimum) × heat, season-length and planting stress.
Yield potential: dry Plains states use approximate irrigated-practice yields; other states use state (or USDA NASS county) averages × 1.1, since average farm yields reach about 85–90% of potential.
Nitrogen, seed and other input costs scale with the expected yield (yield-goal method), so low-yield rain-fed crops are budgeted more cheaply.
Fallow (a season with no crop, only weed control at about $45/acre) is offered only on rain-fed fields with under about 25 inches of rain a year.
Irrigated fields: water need is met and about $110/acre pumping cost is added.
Prices, costs, yield potentials and rotation yield effects are approximate defaults in src/engine/crops.ts and src/engine/regions.ts; replace them with local budgets.
Winter wheat cannot be sown for the first plan year once its fall planting window has passed.
Water: full irrigation. Pumping costs about $8 per inch of water per acre.
Bad years out of 10: how often a crop would have been badly stressed when replayed through the 35 years of NASA weather (shifted to today's climate trends), averaged over the plan's crops.
Yield potential is calibrated to real USDA NASS harvests for irrigated fields: recent average ÷ the share of potential the model says recent weather allowed (kept within 60–115% of the state value).
Corn yield basis: USDA Southwest district average for irrigated fields, 3 reports up to 2018.
Soybean yield basis: county average for 2 recent years × 103% (how irrigated fields compared with all fields in 10 years of county records).
Winter wheat yield basis: USDA Southwest district average for irrigated fields, 4 reports up to 2019.
Grain sorghum yield basis: county average for 2 recent years × 154% (how irrigated fields compared with all fields in 17 years of county records).
Prices: USDA NASS prices received, average of the latest months — corn $4.19/bu (state, 12 months to Sep 2026), soybean $10.88/bu (state, 12 months to Sep 2026), winter wheat $5.38/bu (state, 12 months to Sep 2026), oats $3.14/bu (national, 12 months to Sep 2026), alfalfa (hay) $123.83/ton (state, 12 months to Sep 2026), grain sorghum $3.62/bu (state, 12 months to Sep 2026). cases.text:
English
Español

SOILSENSE · NASA SPACE APPS 2026

Cómo funciona

De observaciones públicas de la Tierra a una rotación de cultivos que puedes cuestionar. El planificador calcula; la IA ayuda a explicar. Ninguno sustituye tu criterio ni el asesoramiento agronómico local.

Arquitectura y flujo de datos
Cuando pides un plan
Agricultor · navegador / teléfono
Archivos estáticos · panel React
API Worker · web + Twilio
Planificador · cálculo, no IA
Explicación del plan · RAG
Sprout · herramientas
Agente telefónico · herramientas
AI Gateway → Workers AI
Gemini · teléfono / respaldo
Caché D1 · textos en Vectorize
Trabajo en segundo plano
Cron · cada hora y cada día
Field Watch · Agents SDK
Durable Objects · revisiones
Workflow de actualización NASA
Obtener → validar → publicar
Evidencia R2 + registros D1
Vectorize · contexto opcional
Ampliar la biblioteca de investigación
Carga en R2 · docs/
Evento de creación en R2
Cola · soilsense-docs
Workflow de documentos
Extraer → dividir → hash
Revisión humana · aprobación
Workers AI · vectores vía Gateway
Vectorize + textos fuente en D1
Las flechas muestran el flujo de datos o solicitudes. El panel de segundo plano contiene tareas programadas paralelas; no todos los servicios llaman al siguiente recuadro. Más detalles en la alternativa textual.
Leer el diagrama como texto
Qué hace cada producto de Cloudflare
Productos seleccionados de wrangler.jsonc; los enlaces describen la configuración, no demuestran un despliegue activo. Las notificaciones son configuración de cuenta documentada en INGEST.md; AI Gateway se selecciona en el código, no mediante un enlace independiente. wrangler.jsonc · INGEST.md
Producto / enlace	Uso en SoilSense
Workers	API Hono, motor determinista de rotaciones, webhooks de Twilio y WebSocket telefónico.
Static assets
ASSETS
	ASSETS sirve el panel React compilado; las solicitudes de API y voz pasan primero por el Worker.
D1
DB
	DB: caché de fuentes, planes/llamadas, registros de actualización, textos de documentos y revisiones.
R2 + event notifications
EVIDENCE
DOCS
	EVIDENCE guarda paquetes NASA con huella; DOCS guarda cargas, texto extraído y manifiestos. Las notificaciones de creación en DOCS alimentan la cola (configuración de cuenta).
Queues
DOC_QUEUE
	DOC_QUEUE / soilsense-docs almacena notificaciones R2 e inicia un Workflow por versión; reintentos limitados, sin cola de mensajes fallidos configurada.
Workflows
POWER_REFRESH
DOC_INGEST
	POWER_REFRESH obtiene, valida y publica registros NASA; DOC_INGEST extrae/divide documentos, espera revisión e indexa el texto aprobado.
Durable Objects / Agents SDK
LIVE_ROOM
FIELD_AGENT
	FIELD_AGENT: Agents SDK, un agente Field Watch con SQLite por parcela vigilada. LIVE_ROOM transmite eventos de llamadas y revisiones al panel.
Cron Triggers	17 * * * * revisa las parcelas cada hora; 43 5 * * * inicia la actualización NASA a las 05:43 UTC cada día.
Workers AI
AI
	AI ejecuta preguntas del plan, Sprout, explicaciones y vectores de investigación; toMarkdown convierte PDF. El planificador no es un modelo de IA.
Vectorize
RESEARCH_INDEX
	RESEARCH_INDEX busca textos por cultivo para explicaciones, conversaciones y notas opcionales de Field Watch. El texto exacto permanece en el corpus o D1.
AI Gateway	AI Gateway se pasa en las opciones de Workers AI (AI_GATEWAY_ID, con valores predeterminados por ruta); no es un enlace de wrangler. Centraliza la observación de solicitudes; las llamadas sin ID configurado ni predeterminado por ruta lo omiten.
Rate Limiting
SCOUT_LIMITER
	SCOUT_LIMITER limita Sprout a 20 solicitudes por IP de visitante por minuto; no es una cuota universal de API.
De dónde vienen los datos
Abajo se distinguen los datos principales, la evidencia opcional y las capas solo cartográficas. Una consulta puntual no es una medición de la parcela. El planificador acepta ubicaciones de los Estados Unidos contiguos.
Fuente	Uso en SoilSense	Límites y alcance
NASA GRACE / GRACE-FO · JPL mascons	Anomalías regionales guardadas del agua total, comparadas descriptivamente con pozos seleccionados de Kansas.	Solo demostración de Finney; soporte de mascon de unos 3°, no píxeles independientes de parcela de 0.5°. Incluye agua del suelo, superficial y nieve, no solo acuíferos.
Kansas Geological Survey · WIZARD	Mediciones guardadas de pozos emparejadas por mes disponible con GRACE en la demostración de Finney.	Pozos cercanos seleccionados; los meses ausentes siguen ausentes. Coincidir en dirección no valida un mascon ni predice tu pozo.
SoilSense Kansas · R2	Un modelo independiente basado solo en clima ordena rotaciones de secano de K-State como segunda opinión y aporta contexto de condado a Field Watch.	Solo Kansas; no es el planificador principal ni garantía de rentabilidad. Revisa la fecha de datos; se identifica la copia guardada si falla el archivo remoto.
NASA POWER	Lluvia, temperatura y humedad radicular diarias; tendencias históricas y simulación de estrés.	Malla MERRA-2 de 0.5° × 0.625° (unos 50–55 km), no estación de la parcela; historial desde 1991.
NASA / ORNL Daymet	Clima principal: se promedia con POWER si está disponible; si no, solo POWER.	Malla de 1 km derivada de estaciones de Norteamérica; no es una medición de la parcela.
USDA NRCS SSURGO	Drenaje, textura, pH, materia orgánica y capacidad de agua disponible del suelo.	Unidades cartográficas de suelo de EE. UU., no análisis reciente; se usan valores típicos si faltan datos.
USDA Cropland Data Layer	Consulta del historial reciente de cultivos para continuar la rotación.	Clasificación anual de 30 m; solo EE. UU.; el agricultor debe confirmar el cultivo actual.
USDA NASS Quick Stats	Rendimientos de condado y precios opcionales; los rendimientos registrados también permiten validar sin conexión.	Requiere NASS_API_KEY en ejecución. Promedios de condado, no de parcela; registros recientes pueden mezclar riego y secano.
USDA RMA Cause of Loss	Registros guardados de pérdidas aseguradas por condado contextualizan las malas cosechas.	Indemnizaciones de condado, no todas las pérdidas ni estrés medido en esta parcela.
OpenET	Comprobación opcional de evapotranspiración y contexto de riego; validación independiente registrada del uso de agua.	Requiere OPENET_API_KEY en ejecución; píxeles puntuales de 30 m desde 2016. El resultado del 6% corresponde a una parcela de Kansas.
FCC Area API	Consulta de condado / FIPS para identificar la ubicación y vincular estadísticas.	Geografía administrativa de EE. UU., no límites de parcela.
Zippopotam.us	Consulta de ubicación por código postal para el planificador, Sprout y llamadas.	La ubicación postal es aproximada; confirma la parcela en el mapa.
U.S. Drought Monitor	Contexto semanal de sequía por condado junto a Field Watch y evidencia histórica.	Estadísticas de superficie por condado; el contexto regional no confirma sequía en la parcela.
NASA MODIS MOD13Q1.061 / ORNL DAAC	Evidencia histórica complementaria del verdor (NDVI), con control estricto de calidad.	Píxel puntual nominal de 250 m, compuestos de 16 días; cobertura de parcela desconocida. NDVI bajo no prueba suelo desnudo; sin datos no equivale a cero.
NASA SMAP SPL4SMGP v008	Evidencia guardada de humedad del suelo con procedencia para ubicaciones de demostración.	Estimaciones asimiladas de 9 km y 3 horas; solo subconjunto de Finney. No es sonda de parcela ni entrada a la clasificación de rotaciones.
NASA GIBS · MODIS Terra	Fondo satelital solo cartográfico para localizar la parcela.	Las imágenes en color real no calculan las puntuaciones de rotación ni miden humedad del suelo.
USGS National Map	Imágenes aéreas de detalle solo cartográficas para encontrar bordes de parcela.	Ayuda para ubicarse, no observación de historial ni salud de cultivos usada por el planificador.
OpenStreetMap	Carreteras, pueblos y nombres de lugares solo cartográficos.	Contexto cartográfico, no entrada agronómica ni límite de parcela levantado por topografía.
K-State · limited-irrigation rotations	Investigación textual seleccionada para explicaciones con citas y herramientas de agentes.	Tribune, Kansas; siembra directa y riego limitado de 10 pulgadas/año. Contexto, no recomendación universal.
K-State · Corn Rootworms	Investigación seleccionada sobre gusano de la raíz del maíz y rotación.	Contexto regional de extensión; la relevancia de búsqueda no es confianza agronómica.
SARE · Building Soils for Better Crops	Textos seleccionados sobre diversificación de sistemas de cultivo.	Contexto general; no demuestra que una parcela obtendrá una rentabilidad concreta.

USGS National Map · OpenStreetMap · RESEARCH.md

Cómo comprobamos los resultados

Prueba registrada fuera de muestra: modelo fijado antes de evaluar, 13 condados no usados antes, 43 casos de condado y cultivo, cuatro cultivos y 12–35 años por caso. Compara rendimientos de condado sin tendencia con estimaciones históricas, no pronósticos de la próxima temporada.

0.41 de correlación de Pearson media
42 de 43 casos: correlación positiva (dirección correcta)
33 de 43 casos superan usar solo lluvia (media de 0.41 frente a 0.21)
OpenET: uso medio de agua modelado dentro del 6% en una parcela con pivote central de Finney, Kansas, 2016–2024; correlación interanual de 0.88

Los promedios de condado no miden la precisión por parcela. Los registros recientes pueden mezclar riego y secano. El trigo de invierno es el cultivo más débil; aún no hay revisión de agricultores ni agrónomos. OpenET es una comprobación independiente del uso de agua en una sola parcela, no una validación de todas las rotaciones. El análisis exploratorio de Field Watch es independiente y no establece la precisión de alertas en vivo.

cases.text:
DATA SOURCES

Where our data comes from

Every plan is built from free, public data from NASA and the US government. Here is each source, what we take from it, and what it does in your plan.

Field data

We look these up live for the exact spot you pick, then cache the results so repeat visits are fast.

NASA POWER

NASA Langley Research Center

Daily weather for any point on Earth, built from NASA satellite and weather-model data (MERRA-2). It covers 1991 to last year.

DATA WE GET
Daily rainfall
Daily average, high and low temperature
Root-zone soil wetness
WHAT IT DOES

This is the core of every plan. From it we work out frost-free days, growing degree days, hot days of 95 °F or more, spring rain, summer dry spells and summer highs. Then we test which of those are really changing on your field.

Visit source ↗
Daymet

NASA Oak Ridge National Laboratory DAAC

Daily weather for North America on a fine 1-kilometer grid, built from weather stations. It covers 1991 to last year.

DATA WE GET
Daily rainfall
Daily high and low temperature
WHAT IT DOES

We average it with NASA POWER for every weather calculation. Two independent NASA datasets agree better with real harvests than either one alone.

Visit source ↗
SSURGO soil survey

USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service

The official US soil map. It is drawn field by field from on-the-ground soil surveys.

DATA WE GET
Soil name and type
Drainage class
pH
Organic matter
Clay and sand content
Water-holding capacity
WHAT IT DOES

This shows how much water your soil can store for dry spells, and which crops suit your soil.

Visit source ↗
Cropland Data Layer (CropScape)

USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service

A satellite map of what was planted on every 30-meter square of US farmland, made every year.

DATA WE GET
What crop grew on your field in each of the last 6 years
WHAT IT DOES

It shows your recent rotation, so the plan follows on from what you actually grew and avoids repeating crops.

Visit source ↗
FCC Area API

Federal Communications Commission

Turns a map point into a US county.

DATA WE GET
County name
State
County code (FIPS)
WHAT IT DOES

We use it to label your field and match it to county-level farm statistics.

Visit source ↗
Quick Stats

USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service

Official USDA farm survey results.

DATA WE GET
County yields, split into irrigated and rain-fed
Crop prices farmers received over the last 12 months
WHAT IT DOES

Sets realistic yields for how your field is farmed, uses current prices for the profit estimates, and provides the real harvests we check our model against.

Visit source ↗
Cause of Loss records

USDA Risk Management Agency

Crop insurance payouts in each county, by crop, year and cause.

DATA WE GET
What hurt each crop in each year: drought, flood, hail, wind, freeze or pests
WHAT IT DOES

Labels the worst harvest years with their real cause, explains years our weather model misses (like the 2020 Iowa windstorm), and adds a "what hurts this crop here" reason.

Visit source ↗
OpenET

OpenET (NASA, USGS, Google and partners), from Landsat satellites

How much water each field actually used each month, measured from satellites since 2016.

DATA WE GET
Monthly water use (evapotranspiration) on your field
WHAT IT DOES

An independent check of our water model, and a hint when a field marked rain-fed is probably irrigated.

Visit source ↗
Zippopotam.us

Open ZIP code database

Turns a US ZIP code into a location.

DATA WE GET
Town
State
Latitude and longitude
WHAT IT DOES

Used by the phone line and by Sprout, so you can say a ZIP code instead of clicking a map.

Visit source ↗
Maps

Map pictures only. These help you find your field and are not used to build the plan.

NASA GIBS (MODIS Terra)

NASA Earth Science Data Systems

Map picture only

True-color satellite pictures of the whole country from NASA's Terra satellite.

DATA WE GET
Satellite picture from a clear midsummer day
WHAT IT DOES

The map you see when it is zoomed out.

Visit source ↗
USGS National Map imagery

US Geological Survey

Map picture only

Detailed aerial photos.

DATA WE GET
Close-up aerial photo
WHAT IT DOES

The map when you zoom in, so you can see the edges of your field.

Visit source ↗
OpenStreetMap

OpenStreetMap contributors

Map picture only

A free street map of the world.

DATA WE GET
Roads
Towns
Place names
WHAT IT DOES

The "Street map" option in the map's layer menu.

Visit source ↗
AI helpers

These only answer your questions. They never change the numbers in your plan.

Workers AI (Llama 3.3)

Cloudflare

Answers questions

An AI model that runs on Cloudflare.

DATA WE GET
Written answers
WHAT IT DOES

Powers Sprout, the chat assistant, and answers the "Have a question?" box. Every call goes through Cloudflare AI Gateway (logs, caching, limits).

Visit source ↗
Gemini

Google

Answers questions

An AI model from Google.

DATA WE GET
Chat answers
WHAT IT DOES

Backup for Sprout if Workers AI is unavailable, and the phone voice agent. Uses the same field data and plan engine as the planner.
